common_name: Cityline Paris Hydrangea (Compact Rose-Red Mophead Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Cityline Paris holds warm rose-red to pink tones even in fairly acidic soil, shifting toward purple-blue only in strongly acidic conditions.

directions: Cityline Paris is a compact bigleaf hydrangea in the city-named Cityline series, bred for a dense, rounded habit under 3 feet tall with sturdy stems that hold large mophead blooms upright rather than flopping, a common problem in older, taller cultivars. Its flowers lean toward warm rose-red and pink tones across a wider soil pH range than many macrophylla cultivars, shifting toward purple only in strongly acidic soil; adding garden lime nudges color pinker, while soil sulfur or aluminum sulfate pushes it bluer. Keep soil consistently moist and humus-rich in partial shade, since the large leaves wilt quickly in dry heat or strong sun. Prune only lightly to remove dead wood, since flowers form primarily on the previous season's growth and heavy pruning sacrifices the coming year's bloom.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Compact Bigleaf Hydrangea Series

common_name: Cityline Venice Hydrangea (Compact Blue-Purple Mophead Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Cityline Venice develops the strongest blue-purple color in acidic soil and shifts toward pink-purple as soil pH rises.

directions: Cityline Venice is a compact bigleaf hydrangea in the Cityline series, holding a dense, well-proportioned habit under 3 feet with strong stems that support its large mophead blooms without flopping. Flower color runs from rich blue-purple in acidic soil to a more muted pinkish-purple as soil pH rises, following the same aluminum-availability color response typical of macrophylla hydrangeas, and can be nudged bluer with soil sulfur or aluminum sulfate. Its compact size fits foundation plantings, small garden beds, and large containers where full-sized hydrangeas would quickly outgrow the space. Keep soil consistently moist and humus-rich in partial shade, and prune only lightly to remove dead wood, since this cultivar blooms mainly on the previous season's growth.

common_name: Wee Bit Giddy Hydrangea (Dwarf Reblooming Pink-Purple Mophead Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; like its sibling Wee Bit Grumpy, Giddy blooms on both old and new wood, giving reliable rebloom through summer even after a late frost damages overwintered buds.

directions: Wee Bit Giddy is a dwarf, reblooming mophead hydrangea sized for a large container or small foundation bed, part of the same extra-compact Wee Bit series as Wee Bit Grumpy. Its rounded flower heads shift between pink and purple depending on soil pH, following the typical macrophylla color response — bluer in acidic soil, pinker as soil becomes more neutral to alkaline. Because it flowers on both old and new wood, damage to overwintered buds from a late spring freeze does not prevent a strong summer rebloom. Keep soil consistently moist in partial shade, since the broad leaves wilt quickly in dry heat, and limit pruning to removing dead wood so the earliest old-wood flowers are not sacrificed.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Dwarf Reblooming Hydrangea Cultivars
Clemson Cooperative Extension — Hydrangea Selection for the South

common_name: Wee Bit Innocent Hydrangea (Dwarf Reblooming White Mophead Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Wee Bit Innocent's white blooms are largely unaffected by soil pH, unlike the blue/pink shifting colors of its Wee Bit series siblings.

directions: Wee Bit Innocent is a dwarf, reblooming mophead hydrangea with clean white flower heads that age to a soft pink-green blush late in the season, on a compact plant sized for a large container or small foundation bed. Because white hydrangea flowers lack the pigment that responds to soil aluminum, its color stays largely consistent regardless of soil pH, unlike the blue-to-pink shifting typical of the genus. Like other Wee Bit series hydrangeas it blooms on both old and new wood, so a late spring freeze that damages overwintered buds does not prevent a solid summer rebloom. Keep soil consistently moist and humus-rich in partial shade, and prune only to remove dead wood so next season's old-wood flowers are preserved.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Dwarf Reblooming Hydrangea Cultivars
